claim: More than 60% of existing infectious diseases of humans are multi-host pathogens (i.e. moving between non-human and human populations).
source: More than 60% of existing infectious diseases of humans are multi-host pathogens (i.e. moving between non-human and human populations) and approximately 75% of emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases affecting humans have a non-human origin (Taylor et al., 2001; van Doorn, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taylor et al., 2001 and van Doorn, 2014.

claim: Approximately 75% of emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases affecting humans have a non-human origin.
source: More than 60% of existing infectious diseases of humans are multi-host pathogens (i.e. moving between non-human and human populations) and approximately 75% of emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases affecting humans have a non-human origin (Taylor et al., 2001; van Doorn, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taylor et al., 2001 and van Doorn, 2014.

claim: Ross River virus (RRV) is responsible for the greatest number of mosquito-borne human disease notifications in Australia, with approximately 5000 cases notified annually.
source: As a case study, we focus on RRV, an alphavirus that causes a disease syndrome characterized by polyarthritis, which is responsible for the greatest number of mosquito-borne human disease notifications in Australia, with approximately 5000 cases notified annually (Australian Govt. Dept. of Health, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Australian Govt. Dept. of Health, 2020.

claim: RRV has caused major epidemics in Pacific Islands involving tens of thousands of cases.
source: It has also caused major epidemics in Pacific Islands involving tens of thousands of cases (Aaskov et al., 1981; Tesh et al., 1981; Harley et al., 2001), and may have the potential to emerge and cause explosive epidemics out of its current geographical range (Flies et al., 2018; Shanks, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aaskov et al., 1981; Tesh et al., 1981; Harley et al., 2001.

claim: More than 15 species of mosquitoes from at least five genera have demonstrated the physiological ability to transmit RRV under controlled laboratory conditions.
source: Under controlled laboratory conditions, more than 15 species of mosquitoes from at least five genera have demonstrated the physiological ability to transmit RRV.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the manuscript without specific citation, suggesting it is established knowledge in the field.

claim: More than 50 species have demonstrated serological evidence of natural exposure to RRV.
source: However, the most important vertebrate hosts of RRV are highly ambiguous because more than 50 species have demonstrated serological evidence of natural exposure to RRV (reviewed in Stephenson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review by Stephenson et al., 2018.

claim: Rats and macropods had the strongest viremic response to RRV infection among vertebrate species available for analysis in Brisbane.
source: Of the vertebrate species available for the analysis in Brisbane, we estimated that rats and macropods had the strongest viremic response to RRV infection (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sheep, rabbits, humans, and possums formed a distinct cluster of hosts with the next strongest viremic responses after rats and macropods.
source: Sheep, rabbits, humans, and possums formed a distinct cluster of hosts with the next strongest responses; uncertainty in host titer profiles obscures our ability to differentiate among the responses of these species.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data and titer profiles.

claim: No dogs or cats developed detectable viremia when exposed to RRV experimentally (N = 10 for each species).
source: No dogs or cats developed detectable viremia when exposed to RRV experimentally (N = 10 for each species), resulting in the lowest physiological competence.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data with specific sample sizes provided.

claim: Coquillettidia linealis was estimated to have the highest physiological potential for RRV transmission among mosquito species.
source: We estimated that the mosquito species with the highest physiological potential for RRV transmission (susceptibility of mosquitoes to infection, and of those that become infected, their potential to transmit RRV) was Coquillettidia linealis, although the 95% CI for this species overlaps with four species with the next highest median estimates (Aedes procax, Verrallina funerea, Aedes vigilax, and Mansonia uniformis) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental infection data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Culex annulirostris, Culex quinquefasciatus, Aedes notoscriptus, and Culex sitiens were estimated to all have low physiological potential for RRV transmission.
source: In contrast, Culex annulirostris, Culex quinquefasciatus, Aedes notoscriptus, and Culex sitiens were estimated to all have low physiological potential.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental infection data.

claim: Humans have the largest estimated median and highest estimated potential for infecting mosquitoes in Brisbane despite large uncertainty.
source: Despite large uncertainty in estimates for the number of mosquitoes that a single infected host can infect while infectious, humans have both the largest estimated median and highest estimated potential (upper 95% CI bound) for infecting mosquitoes in Brisbane.
evidence: This claim is based on modeling results that integrate physiological competence with ecological factors.

claim: An infected human would predominantly infect Ae. vigilax, followed by Ae. procax and Cx. annulirostris.
source: We predict that an infected human would predominantly infect Ae. vigilax, followed by Ae. procax and Cx. annulirostris.
evidence: This is a prediction based on modeling results integrating physiological and ecological data.

claim: Rats and macropods dropped beneath possums, birds, and horses in importance when ecological factors were considered, despite having the highest physiological potential for transmission.
source: Both rats and macropods, which had the highest physiological potential for transmission (Figure 2A), dropped beneath possums, birds, and horses according to median estimates, though overlapping 95% CIs obscure our ability to determine which host is able to infect more mosquitoes while infectious.
evidence: This claim is based on comparing physiological competence (Figure 2A) with half-cycle transmission results that include ecological factors.

claim: Cq. linealis, Ae. procax, Ae. vigilax, and Ve. funerea were estimated to infect the largest number of hosts after embedding mosquito physiological competence into vector-to-host transmission.
source: Cq. linealis, Ae. procax, Ae. vigilax, and Ve. funerea were estimated to infect the largest number of hosts (using median estimates) after embedding mosquito physiological competence into vector-to-host transmission (Figure 3B), although wide overlapping 95% CI make it impossible to differentiate among these species.
evidence: This claim is based on modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An infected Cq. linealis would mostly infect birds.
source: We estimated that an infected Cq. linealis would mostly infect birds, while an infected Ae. procax and Ae. vigilax would infect a larger diversity of host species including birds, humans, and dogs.
evidence: This is a prediction based on modeling results integrating physiological and ecological data.

claim: An infected Ae. procax and Ae. vigilax would infect a larger diversity of host species including birds, humans, and dogs.
source: We estimated that an infected Cq. linealis would mostly infect birds, while an infected Ae. procax and Ae. vigilax would infect a larger diversity of host species including birds, humans, and dogs.
evidence: This is a prediction based on modeling results integrating physiological and ecological data.

claim: Humans, birds, possums, horses, and macropods remained in the top cluster of hosts for complete-cycle transmission.
source: Estimated host importance changed little between host-to-vector and host-vector-host transmission: humans, birds, possums, horses, and macropods remained in the top cluster of hosts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on modeling results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mosquitoes that would acquire RRV from humans mostly go on to infect humans ('self-infections'), followed by birds, dogs, and to a lesser extent possums.
source: We estimated that the mosquitoes that would acquire RRV from humans mostly go on to infect humans ('self-infections'), followed by birds, dogs, and to a lesser extent possums.
evidence: This is a prediction based on modeling results from the next-generation matrix approach.

claim: An infected bird would primarily infect other birds, followed by dogs and humans.
source: We predicted that an infected bird (the species with the second highest estimated median) would primarily infect other birds, followed by dogs and humans, respectively (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a prediction based on modeling results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Humans remained in the top cluster of hosts for RRV transmission potential even when human titer duration was reduced to reflect only the observed human viremic period.
source: Even when human titer duration was reduced, humans remained in the top cluster of hosts (with birds, possums, horses, and macropods) for RRV transmission potential despite an overall lower total number of second-generation infections (Appendix 2—figure 3, Appendix 2—figure 4).
evidence: This claim is based on sensitivity analysis results shown in Appendix 2—figure 3 and Appendix 2—figure 4.

claim: Humans likely contribute to the RRV transmission cycle in Brisbane due to their physiological competence, abundance, and attractiveness to competent mosquitoes like Ae. vigilax and Ae. procax.
source: This highlights the robust result that humans likely contribute to the RRV transmission cycle in Brisbane due to their physiological competence, abundance, and attractiveness to competent mosquitoes like Ae. vigilax and Ae. procax.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple modeling results including sensitivity analyses.

claim: Cq. linealis, Ae. procax, Ve. funerea, Ae. vigilax, and Ma. uniformis have a much higher maximum transmission potential than Cx. annulirostris, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Cx. sitiens, and Ae. notoscriptus for vector-host-vector transmission.
source: Nonetheless, the results suggest that Cq. linealis, Ae. procax, Ve. funerea, Ae. vigilax, and Ma. uniformis have a much higher maximum transmission potential than Cx. annulirostris, Cx. quinquefasciatus, Cx. sitiens, and Ae. notoscriptus.
evidence: This claim is based on modeling results for complete-cycle vector-host-vector transmission.

claim: Most second generation mosquito infections will be in Ae. vigilax, followed by Ae. procax and Cq. linealis, regardless of the species of the originally infected mosquito.
source: For example, regardless of the species of the originally infected mosquito (rows of the Figure 3C matrix), we predict that most second generation infections will be in Ae. vigilax, followed by Ae. procax and Cq. linealis (columns of the Figure 3C matrix), because of their abundance and feeding preferences.
evidence: This is a prediction based on modeling results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ve. funerea and Ma. uniformis are unlikely to play an important role in RRV transmission over multiple generations due to their rarity (0.27% and 0.14% of the Brisbane mosquito community, respectively).
source: Similarly, while an individual Ve. funerea or Ma. uniformis mosquito could potentially have the highest ability for producing second-generation infections in mosquitoes (Figure 3C), their rarity (0.27% and 0.14% of the Brisbane mosquito community, respectively; Supplementary file 2) means that few second generation infections from any source mosquito occur in Ve. funerea or Ma. uniformis. Thus, unlike Ae. vigilax, Ae. procax, and Cq. linealis, the rare mosquitoes Ve. funerea or Ma. uniformis are very unlikely to play an important role in RRV transmission over multiple generations in this ecological context.
evidence: This claim is based on modeling results combined with empirical abundance data from Supplementary file 2.

claim: Starting with one initially infected human in an otherwise susceptible vertebrate population in Brisbane, infections tend to propagate through humans, birds, dogs, and horses.
source: Simulating the spread of infection over multiple generations, starting with one initially infected human in an otherwise susceptible vertebrate population in Brisbane, shows that infections tend to propagate through humans, birds, dogs, and horses (median estimates: Figure 4; estimates with uncertainty: Appendix 2—figure 5).
evidence: This is a prediction based on multi-generation modeling results shown in Figure 4 and Appendix 2—figure 5.

claim: By the third generation of infection, the most dominant pathways of transmission have converged to birds infecting other birds, humans infecting other humans, humans infecting birds, horses infecting humans, and 'wasted' transmissions from both humans and birds to dogs.
source: Overall, while infection does circulate largely in the broader vertebrate community (as opposed to continuously cycling between a small subset of vectors and hosts), we estimated that at the beginning of an epidemic in Brisbane, many infections would occur in humans and birds, a moderate number in horses, and many sink infections in dogs. These new infected individuals (apart from dogs and cats) continue to spread infection in the community, and already by the third generation of infection, the most dominant pathways of transmission have converged to birds infecting other birds, humans infecting other humans, humans infecting birds, horses infecting humans, and 'wasted' transmissions from both humans and birds to dogs, a dead-end host (Figure 4 Generation 3).
evidence: This is a prediction based on multi-generation modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Starting with an initial infection in a Ma. uniformis mosquito, after only a single generation the majority of infected mosquitoes will be Ae. vigilax and Ae. procax, and to a lesser extent Cq. linealis and Cx. annulirostris.
source: Starting with an initial infection in a Ma. uniformis mosquito (to illustrate the effect of beginning with an infection in a rare species), the multi-generation approximation shows that after only a single generation the framework predicts that the majority of infected mosquitoes will be Ae. vigilax and Ae. procax, and to a lesser extent Cq. linealis and Cx. annulirostris (median estimates: Figure 4; estimates with uncertainty: Appendix 2—figure 6), which mirrors the results in Figure 3C.
evidence: This is a prediction based on multi-generation modeling results shown in Figure 4 and Appendix 2—figure 6.

claim: After only three generations, most transmission of RRV in Brisbane was occurring from Ae. vigilax, Ae. procax, and Cq. linealis.
source: After only three generations, we predicted that most transmission of RRV in Brisbane was occurring from Ae. vigilax, Ae. procax, and Cq. linealis; the dominance of these three species can be seen in Figure 4 by the large number of pairwise transmission events between them.
evidence: This is a prediction based on multi-generation modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The findings for RRV transmission cycles in Brisbane point to two overlapping transmission cycles: an enzootic cycle, characterized primarily by transmission between birds and Cq. linealis, and a domestic cycle characterized by human-to-human infections facilitated by Ae. vigilax and Ae. procax.
source: Despite large uncertainty, our findings for RRV transmission cycles in Brisbane point to two overlapping transmission cycles: an enzootic cycle, characterized primarily by transmission between birds and Cq. linealis, and a domestic cycle characterized by human-to-human infections facilitated by Ae. vigilax and Ae. procax.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results across multiple analyses.

claim: The two transmission cycles (enzootic and domestic) are linked by feeding generalists, which transfer infection between birds and humans.
source: These two cycles are linked by these feeding generalists, which transfer infection between birds and humans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results on mosquito feeding patterns and transmission.

claim: Dogs play a diluting role by absorbing infectious bites as they are not able to transmit RRV.
source: Within each of these overlapping cycles, dogs play a diluting role by absorbing infectious bites as they are not able to transmit RRV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that dogs do not develop viremia and the modeling results showing 'wasted' transmissions to dogs.

claim: Horses occasionally develop high viremia in response to RRV infection.
source: By contrast, horses, which occasionally develop high viremia in response to RRV infection and have been previously considered a moderately competent host (described in Stephenson et al., 2018), have low physiological competence on average because less than 15% of exposed horses develop a viremic response when infected.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data and is also cited to Stephenson et al., 2018.

claim: Less than 15% of exposed horses develop a viremic response when infected with RRV.
source: By contrast, horses, which occasionally develop high viremia in response to RRV infection and have been previously considered a moderately competent host (described in Stephenson et al., 2018), have low physiological competence on average because less than 15% of exposed horses develop a viremic response when infected.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data.

claim: Humans had a moderate-to-high physiological competence following infection with RRV.
source: Conversely, humans, which have not been considered important for local transmission, had a moderate-to-high physiological competence following infection with RRV (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of titer data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No single mosquito species was dominant in its physiological competence for RRV, supporting the view that RRV is a generalist virus.
source: For vectors, RRV has long been considered a generalist virus, capable of persisting across climates and habitats within Australia; our result that no single species was dominant in its physiological competence supports this view.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results on mosquito physiological competence, combined with established knowledge about RRV.

claim: Humans contributed 66% of the total community abundance in Brisbane, with less than 14% seropositivity.
source: For example, when compared to all other hosts, humans had the highest susceptible population (contributing 66% of the total community abundance, with less than 14% seropositivity).
evidence: This claim is based on empirical abundance and seroprevalence data.

claim: Birds were estimated to be only approximately 5% of the host community composition in Brisbane.
source: In contrast, birds were estimated to be only approximately 5% of the host community composition and almost a third were seropositive, further reducing the total number of susceptible individuals.
evidence: This claim is based on empirical abundance data.

claim: Almost a third of birds in Brisbane were seropositive for RRV.
source: In contrast, birds were estimated to be only approximately 5% of the host community composition and almost a third were seropositive, further reducing the total number of susceptible individuals.
evidence: This claim is based on empirical seroprevalence data.

claim: Birds' high importance in half and complete transmission cycles is likely driven by the strong feeding association with the highly physiologically competent mosquito Cq. linealis rather than birds' physiological competence or abundance.
source: Despite this relative scarcity, birds were highly important in the half and complete transmission cycles. This high importance is likely driven by the strong feeding association with the highly physiologically competent mosquito Cq. linealis rather than birds' physiological competence or abundance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing different modeling results (physiological competence vs. half-cycle and complete-cycle transmission).

claim: A potentially fruitful path for reducing human infections is vector control of Ae. vigilax populations.
source: That being said, the number of Ae. vigilax that humans infect (Figure 2B) suggests that a potentially fruitful path for reducing human infections is vector control of Ae. vigilax populations, which is already one of the primary targets of mosquito control operations in Brisbane (Brisbane City Council,, 2019).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on modeling results, with a citation noting that Ae. vigilax is already targeted in Brisbane.

claim: Ae. vigilax is already one of the primary targets of mosquito control operations in Brisbane.
source: That being said, the number of Ae. vigilax that humans infect (Figure 2B) suggests that a potentially fruitful path for reducing human infections is vector control of Ae. vigilax populations, which is already one of the primary targets of mosquito control operations in Brisbane (Brisbane City Council,, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brisbane City Council, 2019.

claim: Cx. annulirostris and Ae. notoscriptus are less competent vectors than Ae. vigilax, Ae. procax and Cq. linealis, although they are often cited as key RRV vectors in Brisbane.
source: However, we predicted that Cx. annulirostris and Ae. notoscriptus are less competent vectors, although they are often cited as key RRV vectors in Brisbane (Kay and Aaskov, 1989; Russell, 1995; Watson and Kay, 1998).
evidence: This is a prediction based on modeling results, contrasted with previous literature (Kay and Aaskov, 1989; Russell, 1995; Watson and Kay, 1998).

claim: RRV is frequently detected in wild-caught Cx. annulirostris individuals.
source: The evidence in favor of Cx. annulirostris as a vector is that RRV is frequently detected in wild-caught individuals, and that abundance has been high during previous outbreaks of RRV (Jansen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jansen et al., 2019.

claim: Cx. annulirostris abundance has been high during previous outbreaks of RRV.
source: The evidence in favor of Cx. annulirostris as a vector is that RRV is frequently detected in wild-caught individuals, and that abundance has been high during previous outbreaks of RRV (Jansen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jansen et al., 2019.

claim: RRV has been isolated from Ae. notoscriptus during outbreaks in Brisbane.
source: RRV has also been isolated from Ae. notoscriptus during outbreaks in Brisbane (Ritchie et al., 1997); however, the species had relatively low abundance in this study, and low transmission ability (Appendix 1—figure 4) in comparison to other potential vectors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ritchie et al., 1997.

claim: Ae. notoscriptus had relatively low abundance in this study and low transmission ability in comparison to other potential vectors.
source: RRV has also been isolated from Ae. notoscriptus during outbreaks in Brisbane (Ritchie et al., 1997); however, the species had relatively low abundance in this study, and low transmission ability (Appendix 1—figure 4) in comparison to other potential vectors.
evidence: This claim is based on empirical abundance data from this study and modeling results shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: Cx. annulirostris and Ae. notoscriptus are secondary RRV vectors (capable of playing a supplemental role in transmission but unable to maintain an epidemic) to other species such as Ae. vigilax which are primary RRV vectors (capable of starting and maintaining epidemics).
source: This suggests a new hypothesis that Cx. annulirostris and Ae. notoscriptus are secondary RRV vectors (capable of playing a supplemental role in transmission but unable to maintain an epidemic) to other species such as Ae. vigilax which are primary RRV vectors (capable of starting and maintaining epidemics).
evidence: This is a hypothesis generated from the modeling results.

claim: The distinction between primary and secondary vectors has been made for other arboviruses.
source: Although novel for RRV, the distinction between primary and secondary vectors has been made for other arboviruses (Turell et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Turell et al., 2005.

claim: The isolation of RRV from wild caught mosquitoes demonstrates that a particular species is infected with the virus, but is incomplete evidence for mosquito species' specific role in virus transmission.
source: Finally, the isolation of RRV from wild caught mosquitoes demonstrates that a particular species is infected with the virus, it is incomplete evidence for mosquito species' specific role in virus transmission.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of field detection data.

claim: The lower transmission capability of Cx. annulirostris or Ae. notoscriptus relative to Ae. vigilax, Ae. procax and Cq. linealis means that the former are likely to transmit infection to fewer hosts than the latter, even if found infected in the field.
source: Even if found infected in the field, the lower transmission capability of Cx. annulirostris or Ae. notoscriptus relative to Ae. vigilax, Ae. procax and Cq. linealis means that the former are likely to transmit infection to fewer hosts than the latter.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results on transmission capability.

claim: Mosquito survival was modeled as being identical for all species using an exponential decay model with a daily survival probability that is half of the daily maximum survival rate of Cx. annulirostris measured in optimal laboratory conditions.
source: For this reason, we modeled mosquito survival as being identical for all species. Specifically, we used an exponential decay model for mosquito survival using a daily survival probability that is half of the daily maximum survival rate of Cx. annulirostris (calculated as 1/lifespan) measured in optimal laboratory conditions (from Shocket et al., 2018 who used data from McDonald et al., 1980, which may over-estimate survival rates in nature).
evidence: This is a methodological choice based on data from Shocket et al., 2018 and McDonald et al., 1980.

claim: Mosquito survival probability was assumed to fall to zero after day 38.
source: However, we assume that mosquito survival probability falls to zero after day 38.
evidence: This is a stated assumption in the modeling approach.

claim: The overall raw number of mosquitoes per host in the Brisbane community was assumed to be 40.
source: Because the number of mosquitoes per host (Equation 1: ϕ) is needed to calculate the absolute number of mosquitoes an infected host would infect, we multiplied the relative abundances of mosquitoes by 40 (our assumed value for overall raw number of mosquitoes per host in the community).
evidence: This is a stated assumption in the modeling approach.

claim: The three bird species (Pacific black duck, domestic chicken, and little corella) have very similar viremic responses to RRV.
source: This averaging implicitly assumes (in the absence of species-level information) that all birds and all macropods respond identically to infection. Although a strong simplifying assumption, the three bird species have very similar viremic responses, as do the two macropod species (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The two macropod species (agile wallaby and eastern grey kangaroo) have very similar viremic responses to RRV.
source: This averaging implicitly assumes (in the absence of species-level information) that all birds and all macropods respond identically to infection. Although a strong simplifying assumption, the three bird species have very similar viremic responses, as do the two macropod species (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The nine mosquito species retained for analysis account for 90% of the Brisbane mosquito community according to abundance data.
source: Finally, we retained only nine mosquito species for which we had both abundance data and blood meal data (Supplementary file 2), although this excludes many potentially relevant mosquito species, the nine species we retained account for 90% of the Brisbane mosquito community according to our abundance data (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is based on empirical abundance data from Supplementary file 1.

claim: RRV is an alphavirus that causes a disease syndrome characterized by polyarthritis.
source: As a case study, we focus on RRV, an alphavirus that causes a disease syndrome characterized by polyarthritis, which is responsible for the greatest number of mosquito-borne human disease notifications in Australia, with approximately 5000 cases notified annually (Australian Govt. Dept. of Health, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RRV, also supported by citation.

claim: RRV may have the potential to emerge and cause explosive epidemics out of its current geographical range.
source: It has also caused major epidemics in Pacific Islands involving tens of thousands of cases (Aaskov et al., 1981; Tesh et al., 1981; Harley et al., 2001), and may have the potential to emerge and cause explosive epidemics out of its current geographical range (Flies et al., 2018; Shanks, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Flies et al., 2018 and Shanks, 2019.

claim: The disease (RRV) has long been considered to exist in a zoonotic transmission cycle, primarily because the number of human cases during winter months was considered to be too low to sustain community transmission.
source: The disease has long been considered to exist in a zoonotic transmission cycle, primarily because the number of human cases during winter months was considered to be too low to sustain community transmission (Harley et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Harley et al., 2001.

claim: The framework presented accounts for uncertainty from each fitted statistical model in estimates of species' contributions to transmission.
source: The framework accounts for uncertainty from each fitted statistical model in estimates of species' contributions to transmission and has has direct application to other zoonotic pathogens.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The framework has direct application to other zoonotic pathogens.
source: The framework accounts for uncertainty from each fitted statistical model in estimates of species' contributions to transmission and has has direct application to other zoonotic pathogens.
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the framework.

claim: Vertebrate hosts with high physiological competence are not the most important for community transmission of RRV; interactions between hosts and vectors largely underpin the importance of host species.
source: We find that vertebrate hosts with high physiological competence are not the most important for community transmission; interactions between hosts and vectors largely underpin the importance of host species.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the modeling results.

claim: For vectors, physiological competence is highly important for RRV transmission.
source: For vectors, physiological competence is highly important.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the modeling results.

claim: The nested approach integrates species' physiological competence with their ecological traits to quantify the importance of host and vectors.
source: We present a nested approach for quantifying the importance of host and vectors that integrates species' physiological competence with their ecological traits.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claim: The approach uses three nested metrics of increasing biological complexity: physiological competence; transmission over one half of the pathogen's life cycle (half-cycle transmission); and transmission over the pathogen's complete life cycle (complete-cycle transmission).
source: The approach uses three nested metrics of increasing biological complexity: physiological competence; transmission over one half of the pathogen's life cycle (half-cycle transmission; that is, host-to-vector or vector-to-host transmission); and transmission over the pathogen's complete life cycle (complete-cycle transmission) (Box 1).
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claim: A framework that integrates the entire transmission cycle can be useful for hypothesis testing and for guiding data collection by identifying the processes that most contribute to uncertainty in competence.
source: Even for systems with limited data, a framework that integrates the entire transmission cycle can be useful for hypothesis testing and for guiding data collection by identifying the processes that most contribute to uncertainty in competence (i.e. model-guided fieldwork, sensu Restif et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of the framework, with a citation to Restif et al., 2012.

claim: Understanding the ecological importance of host and vector species for transmission requires modeling the complete transmission cycle (host-vector-host or vector-host-vector transmission), 'closing the loop' by estimating the number of new infections in the next generation.
source: Understanding the ecological importance of host and vector species for transmission requires modeling the complete transmission cycle (host-vector-host or vector-host-vector transmission), 'closing the loop' by estimating the number of new infections in the next generation.
evidence: This is a methodological principle stated in the manuscript.

claim: This approach (modeling complete transmission cycles) is used less frequently for multi-vector, multi-host pathogens because of the need for data across multiple phases of transmission for multiple host and vector species.
source: While this is well understood (e.g. see Turner et al., 2013, Fenton et al., 2015, Webster et al., 2017), this approach is used less frequently for multi-vector, multi-host pathogens because of the need for data across multiple phases of transmission for multiple host and vector species.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the field, supported by citations to Turner et al., 2013, Fenton et al., 2015, Webster et al., 2017.

claim: Studies characterising zoonotic arbovirus transmission often focus on pairwise transmission between non-human hosts and vectors, or vectors and humans.
source: Studies characterising zoonotic arbovirus transmission often focus on pairwise transmission between non-human hosts and vectors, or vectors and humans (for example work in WNV: Marm Kilpatrick et al., 2006, Ross River virus: Koolhof and Carver, 2017, Stephenson et al., 2018, leishmaniasis: Stephens et al., 2016, Chagas disease: Gürtler and Cardinal, 2015, Jansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Approaches that capture only a portion of a pathogen's transmission cycle cannot completely quantify a species' contribution to transmission within a community.
source: However, these and other proposed approaches (Appendix 1—table 1) that capture only a portion of a pathogen's transmission cycle cannot completely quantify a species' contribution to transmission within a community.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of partial transmission cycle approaches.

claim: Developing appropriate mitigation strategies for zoonotic pathogens hinges on quantifying which processes have the largest influence over each species' importance in transmission cycles.
source: Developing appropriate mitigation strategies for zoonotic pathogens hinges on quantifying which processes have the largest influence over each species' importance in transmission cycles.
evidence: This is a general principle stated in the manuscript.

claim: Identifying the key vector and host species that drive the transmission of zoonotic pathogens is notoriously difficult but critical for disease control.
source: Identifying the key vector and host species that drive the transmission of zoonotic pathogens is notoriously difficult but critical for disease control.
evidence: This is a general principle stated in the manuscript.

claim: The dynamics of multi-host pathogen systems can range in complexity from spillover between a single source population to a single target population to large interconnected networks of species that maintain a pathogen in a given environment and facilitate spillover into a target population.
source: The dynamics of multi-host pathogen systems can range in complexity from spillover between a single source population to a single target population (e.g. from bats to humans as has been postulated for SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2: Boni et al., 2020) to large interconnected networks of species that maintain a pathogen in a given environment and facilitate spillover into a target population (e.g. zoonotic arboviruses, such as West Nile (WNV) and Rift Valley fever (RVFV) viruses: Viana et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a general principle with examples supported by citations to Boni et al., 2020 and Viana et al., 2014.
